Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant

neck rotation and head shape · ear position and sutures · hips and feet

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Head tilts toward a tight sternocleidomastoid (SCM), chin turns away: congenital muscular torticollis. A firm muscle mass differs from a soft, transilluminating lymphatic malformation.
  • Flat occiput, same-side ear forward: positional plagiocephaly. Ear displaced backward with a suture ridge: suspect lambdoid craniosynostosis and refer for craniofacial evaluation.
  • Stretching and physical therapy, repositioning and awake tummy time; keep supine sleep. Examine hips and feet; a new tilt with neurologic signs needs brain MRI.
What it is

A shortened or fibrotic SCM producing a tilted head usually noticed within the first 3 months

Driver

Intrauterine constraint or neck-muscle injury may contribute

Triggers

Breech positioning or other intrauterine constraint (non-modifiable)

A persistent head-position preference; prematurity increases positional flattening risk

Chain

Restricted neck rotation one-sided positioning pressure-related skull flattening

Insights

The tilt identifies the tight side. The chin points toward the opposite shoulder.

Skull position separates two processes. Forward ear displacement favors pressure-related molding; posterior displacement with a ridge suggests suture fusion.

2Urgent risks
NeurologicNew head tilt in an older child with headache, vomiting or neurologic findings

If a central cause is possible, choose obtain brain MRI to evaluate a posterior fossa lesion.

Suture fusionA posteriorly displaced ear on the flat side with a ridge

If craniosynostosis is suspected, choose refer to a craniofacial or neurosurgical team; confirm the suture abnormality.

3Differential
Head tilt, a flat occiput or a neck mass
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Congenital muscular torticollisEarly infant; tight SCM, tilt toward it and chin awayFirm muscle mass that does not transilluminate; limited neck rotation
Positional plagiocephalyFlat occiput; same-side ear and forehead project forwardA parallelogram shape, without a fused-suture ridge
Lambdoid craniosynostosisFlat occiput with the same-side ear farther backA ridge and trapezoid shape suggest fusion rather than positional molding
Cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation)Soft, fluctuant posterior-triangle massTransilluminates; not a firm contracted SCM
Cervical lymphadenitisTender enlarging node, fever or overlying warmth and rednessInflammation outside the SCM rather than its painless shortening
Posterior fossa tumorAcquired head tilt with neurologic findings in an older childBrain MRI, rather than treating the tilt as an infant muscle contracture
Early infancyCongenital muscle restriction becomes apparent
During growthA one-sided preference can perpetuate skull flattening
4Workup
Imaging pathwayThe 2003 head-deformity pathway recommends skull radiographs after 4 to 8 weeks without improvement, followed by CT if sutures are unclear or appear closed. An uncertain head shape warrants craniofacial or neurosurgical referral.

Pause point. The flat side does not identify the tight SCM. The muscle tilts the head toward itself and rotates the chin away; inspect the ear and forehead separately to classify the skull shape.

5Diagnostic criteria
Clinical findings
FindingInterpretation
Fixed tilt with restricted rotation and a firm SCMMuscular torticollis
Anterior ear displacement and same-side forehead prominencePositional deformity is favored
Posterior ear displacement and a suture ridgeSuture fusion is suspected
6Severity
Findings that change the plan
FindingDo
Persistent neck restriction despite physical therapyRefer to pediatric orthopedics to reassess resistant muscle contracture
Persistent severe skull flatteningConfirm the diagnosis and consider orthotic treatment
A dislocatable hip that reduces with OrtolaniDevelopmental dysplasia of the hip: refer and use age-appropriate treatment, usually a Pavlik harness in infancy
7Treatment
1

Musclea typical congenital SCM contracture

Caregiver-guided gentle stretching and physical therapy
2

Positionpositional flattening or a persistent side preference

Vary carrying and feeding positions; offer supervised awake tummy time; continue back sleeping
3

Escalateneck restriction or skull deformity persists

Specialist reassessment; a helmet may help persistent positional flattening, while resistant muscle contracture needs an orthopedic treatment plan
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
During therapyTrack active neck rotation, tilt and head-shape symmetry
Persistent neck restriction despite therapyReassess the diagnosis and treatment plan with pediatric orthopedics
Atypical progression or new neurologic signsInvestigate another cause rather than continuing stretching alone
Practice
  1. 2-month-old girl, born breech, with a flat right occiput neck mass first felt at 3 weeks; right ear forward head tilts left; chin turns right Firm, painless left sternocleidomastoid mass; does not transilluminate T 37.0 °C · hips stable → Congenital muscular torticollis → tilt toward a firm sternocleidomastoid mass with the chin turned away is congenital muscular torticollis; the flat head with the ear forward is positional, from lying one way; stretching, repositioning, tummy time
  2. 3-month-old girl with a flat right occiput right ear and forehead sit forward sleeps on her back; full neck rotation No neck mass or ridge T 36.9 °C · head circumference 50th percentile → Positional plagiocephaly → a flat occiput with the ear and forehead forward (a parallelogram) is positional plagiocephaly: repositioning and tummy time, no imaging
  3. 4-month-old boy with a flat right occiput right ear sits behind the left palpable ridge over the right lambdoid suture No neck mass; full neck rotation T 37.0 °C · head circumference 40th percentile → Craniosynostosis → a flat occiput with the ear pushed back and a ridge (a trapezoid) is lambdoid craniosynostosis: head CT and craniofacial referral
  4. Newborn girl with a neck mass noted at birth soft, fluctuant, in the posterior triangle the mass transilluminates Head held midline; no tilt T 36.8 °C · feeding and breathing normally → Cystic hygroma → a soft posterior-triangle mass that transilluminates is a cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation), linked to aneuploidy; the torticollis mass is firm and does not transilluminate
  5. 8-year-old boy with 3 weeks of a new head tilt morning headaches; vomits on waking papilledema on fundoscopy Left sixth nerve palsy: cannot abduct the left eye T 37.0 °C · no neck mass or fever → Posterior fossa tumor → a new head tilt with headache, vomiting or neurologic findings needs brain MRI to evaluate a central cause, including a posterior fossa tumor
  6. 2-month-old girl was diagnosed with congenital muscular torticollis today born breech at term head tilts right; chin turns left; firm right sternocleidomastoid mass Feet look normal T 37.0 °C · hip exam equivocal → Hip ultrasound → torticollis and breech can accompany hip dysplasia; the equivocal hip examination in this infant calls for hip ultrasound
  7. 2-month-old girl with a head tilt to the right since birth born breech; firm right sternocleidomastoid mass left hip clunks on Barlow, reduces on Ortolani Left thigh folds asymmetric T 37.0 °C · no hip swelling or warmth → Developmental dysplasia of the hip → a dislocatable hip that reduces in an infant is developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), part of the crowding picture: Pavlik harness; the tilt and mass are the torticollis
  8. 6-month-old girl was diagnosed with congenital muscular torticollis at 2 months 3 months of daily stretching and physical therapy tilt and limited rotation unchanged Sternocleidomastoid still tight T 37.0 °C · no neurologic signs → Refer to pediatric orthopedics → persistent restricted motion despite physical therapy needs pediatric orthopedic reassessment rather than another prolonged course of unchanged therapy
Pairs with Brachial Plexus Injury at Birth: the newborn who will not move an arm. Brain Tumors in a Child: the acquired tilt with cranial nerve signs. Posterior Urethral Valves: the same constraint physiology.
Transferable rule

The underlying cause explains every finding: crowding gives the tilt and the hip, and the tilt gives the flat head; reject a diagnosis that leaves one out.
